622382375.en:
@_**Jacob Lifshay|229517** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/122651-general/topic/False.20positive.20.60deny.28static_mut_refs.29.60/near/622382170):
```quote
note the `A[i]` operation is a compiler built-in (only when `i: usize`) -- it doesn't actually call any library code, unlike the `get_unchecked` function call
```

Does that matter for reference liveness? I would assume it behaves exactly like a library call for e.g. stacked borrows.

@_**Jacob Lifshay|229517** [说](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/122651-general/topic/False.20positive.20.60deny.28static_mut_refs.29.60/near/622382170):

622383489.en: it doesn't create any references, I'm not sure if that makes it behave differently in regards to stacked borrows (I'm too tired at the moment to think it through, sorry)

622408943.en: If there exists a mutable reference to an element of `A` while `a`/`b` is called for a *different* element, `a` does not conflict with that since it only accesses one element, but `b` does conflict since it takes a shared reference to `A` as a whole.  https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=d6e5e38ffdc54fe3c44009e19ec8b0e3 (This example fails under current stacked borrows and tree borrows)
622408943.zh: 如果存在对某个元素的可变引用`A`尽管`a`/`b`被调用为*不同的*元素，`a`与此不冲突，因为它只访问一个元素，但是`b`确实存在冲突，因为它需要共享引用`A`作为一个整体。https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=d6e5e38ffdc54fe3c44009e19ec8b0e3（此示例在当前堆叠借用和树借用下失败）

622500530.en: iirc the documentation is generally something like: "just use it through raw pointers, don't create references to mutable statics".
622500530.zh: iirc 文档通常类似于：“只需通过原始指针使用它，不要创建对可变静态的引用”。

622501133.en: so using `A[i]` technically works because it's a compiler built-in, but it's mostly in the same category as calling methods that implicitly make references and stuff so imo you shouldn't do it on mutable statics, use pointers instead.
622501133.zh: 所以使用`A[i]`从技术上讲，它是有效的，因为它是内置的编译器，但它主要与隐式创建引用和内容的调用方法属于同一类别，因此在我看来，您不应该在可变静态上执行此操作，而应使用指针。

622498443.en:
if that's in reference to `makecontext` only allowing you to pass arguments that are `int`s to the called function, that can be used soundly to pass a pointer, you just have to cast the pointer to `usize`, and then split that into `int`-sized hunks. 

some programmers would pass a `long` or pointer directly, which is UB, though it kinda worked on most 32-bit systems and a few 64-bit systems.
622498443.zh:
如果这是关于`makecontext`仅允许您传递`int`到被调用的函数，可以很好地使用它来传递指针，您只需将指针转换为`usize`，然后将其拆分为`int`-大块头。 

一些程序员会通过一个`long`或指针，这是UB ，尽管它适用于大多数32位系统和少数64位系统。

620377919.en:
So, it certainly sounds like opt-level=1 is doing its job, of being an optimization level that makes things noticeably faster without taking as much time as opt-level 2 or 3 to compile.

But that doesn't make it a good default for `dev`. `dev` should build as fast as possible. It should do any optimizations that *make the code faster to compile*, but it already does; opt-level 0 includes some MIR optimizations that are faster than not doing them, because they result in doing less work in compilation.
620377919.zh:
因此，听起来 opt-level=1 确实正在发挥作用，作为一个优化级别，它可以使事情明显更快，而无需花费像 opt-level 2 或 3 那么多的时间来编译。

但这并不能使它成为一个很好的默认值`dev`。`dev`应该尽快构建。它应该做任何优化来*使代码编译速度更快*，但它已经这样做了； opt-level 0 包含一些比不执行更快的 MIR 优化，因为它们会减少编译工作。

620378127.en: If people *want* to turn on optimizations on `dev`, they can. But our defaults should aim for fast builds.
620378127.zh: 如果人们“想要”开启优化`dev`，他们可以。但我们的默认设置应该以快速构建为目标。

620379492.en: opt-level=0 has a dual purpose of compiling as fast as possible and giving maximum debugging fidelity. When these are in conflict you have to pick one or the other. We may have some MIR passes right now that vary behavior based on debug info level but at least in LLVM it's explicit policy to not do that. Between that and "opt level < 0" looking silly, I think it's better to call the "compile as fast as possible at expense of debuggability" optimization level something different than "0" (assuming this level can realistically exist at all).
620379492.zh: opt-level=0 有双重目的：尽可能快地编译并提供最大的调试保真度。当这些发生冲突时，你必须选择其中之一。我们现在可能有一些 MIR 通道，它们会根据调试信息级别改变行为，但至少在 LLVM 中，明确的策略是不这样做。在这和看起来很愚蠢的“opt level < 0”之间，我认为最好将“以牺牲可调试性为代价尽可能快地编译”优化级别称为与“0”不同的东西（假设这个级别实际上可以存在）。

Substituting mathematical functions with approximations is a whole other can of worms. There is no guarantee or bound whatsoever on their precision, at least with algebraic ops you know the output is some mathematically equivalent expression were it not for IEEE754's rounding/nans/infinities. They are genuinely useful for (unless the source material was already carefully written) producing faster (autovectorized) and typically more accurate expressions.

A potentially easier question (but if anyone disagrees, probably best to move it to a new thread), is how much we care about errno. This currently seems to be an undocumented implementation detail on the Rust side, based on whether we go through the llvm intrinsic, or the libm call. When writing these papers we had to look at IR differences between what we generate from rustc, and what we get from clang, to figure out where performance differences come from. In c++ we have `-fno-math-errno` to change that, but in Rust it seems like an implementation detail that users can't change: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html#unspecified-precision-23 

My theory is that we used llvm intrinsics when they were (back then) available and libm otherwise. So some of our float operations just prevent DCE, LICM and other opts, while other float intrinsics allow them. I suggest we fix that, as it seems much less controversial than replacing the opts with some approximations.

I made a draft PR to show the differences: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/162104

Note that I'm not doubting that the `algebraic_*` operations help performance. What I'm asking for is the difference for source code readability, ease of authoring, maintainability, etc. of how you access the algebraic operations (`Algebraic<F>` wrapper type with operator overloading vs. the existing methods on primitive types).

From the source code you shared, there's some that seem to hardly use any overloaded operators (e.g. [pressure](https://github.com/ZuseZ4/rust_perf/blob/61da77cf93731c9096583187b82239a26d5e3e8c/src/apps/pressure.rs#L201-L213)) but also some (e.g., [del_dot_vec_2d](https://github.com/ZuseZ4/rust_perf/blob/61da77cf93731c9096583187b82239a26d5e3e8c/src/apps/del_dot_vec_2d.rs#L264-L285) or [matvec_3d_stencil](https://github.com/ZuseZ4/rust_perf/blob/61da77cf93731c9096583187b82239a26d5e3e8c/src/apps/matvec_3d_stencil.rs#L243-L271)) with a lot of `Real` operators. Some thoughts:

1) Those kernels look like a ton of line noise due to all the raw pointer arithmetic interleaved with actual work (no offense, been there done that). I wonder if it's more compelling in code that is overall more tuned for readability and safety.

2) The benchmarks benefits from all the array elements and scalars being typed as `Real` from start to end, so there's no  place where you have to switch back and forth other than for float literals. This makes sense for isolated kernels but is probably less true when embedded in a larger application than a benchmark harness.

    - name: Configure Windows PATH

      run: |

    PATH="$PATH:/mingw32/bin"

fi

pacman -S --noconfirm mingw-w64-i686-gcc
```

I've been working on a GBA game and am using the agb crate to so. As part of it, I have a few types of game objects with common interfaces (update, show, take_damage, position, etc...). In my original implementation, to keep code tidy, I was storing game objects together in vectors of type `Box<dyn Enemy>`, as an example.

When running into performance issues, I had a suspicion that the dyn type to be a culprit, because the main bulk of computational work would be on calling these update functions. So, looking into it, I found the crate [enum_dispatch](https://docs.rs/enum_dispatch/latest/enum_dispatch/), and migrating our `Box<dyn Enemy>` types to the `Enemy` enum did give huge performance gains! The limits are now mostly due to hardware constraints on visible sprite counts as opposed to CPU cycles.

I haven't dug into the assembly, but I suspect the gains are due to compiler optimizations becoming available that couldn't be assumed for the dyn type.

So, I wanted to ask out of interest, why isn't there something like this built into the rust language? I know it's not applicable in all situations, particularly in compiled libraries, but in cases when all types are known at compile time, would it not be possible to eliminate these dynamic dispatched traits? Or, would it not be optimial sometimes? I saw this comment, which referenced this being a potential feature as well: https://github.com/rust-lang/goals/issues/257#issuecomment-3155934755

Genuinely curious about all of this, and would love to learn more and maybe hack away on implementation. It has been a while since my college class on compilers so I'm definitely out of my depth, but I am all ears!

618008854.en: When *I* use dynamic dispatch, I generally use it deliberately to achieve a specific balance of trade-offs, and I would not appreciate the compiler doing heroics behind my back to undo that. Like sure, don't do indirect calls in every iteration of your hot inner loop! But in a well architected program, there are also many calls sites where static dispatch buys you absolutely nothing performance-wise and costs you a lot (in build times, binary size, cognitive complexity, API fragility, etc. etc.)

618011238.en: Regarding cognitive complexity and API fragility, I'm not talking about the boilerplate that `enum_dispatch` helps with. That's trivial in my book (which is also why I'm not a fan of using the crate in my own code). In the narrow case where you can just define an enum, you're just swapping a type involving `dyn Trait` for that enum. But if you want to push static dispatch everywhere, you often end up with a lot of code that's generic over `T: Trait`, and then that easily leads to lots and lots of more bounds, more generics, more type-level programming, to be able to express all the non-trivial things happening with and around that `T`. 616360082.en:
I maintain the [twox-hash](https://crates.io/crates/twox-hash/) crate, which is a native-Rust implementation of the [xxHash](https://xxhash.com) family of algorithms. Some folks from the icu4x team [noticed](https://github.com/unicode-org/icu4x/issues/8356) that hashing a `Vec` produced different results on 32-bit vs 64-bit systems, and opened [an issue for me](https://github.com/shepmaster/twox-hash/issues/123).

The root cause  is that when you hash a `Vec`, it ultimately uses `write_usize` which writes the bytes of the number as a platform-native chunk of bytes. That changes from 32-bit to 64-bit as the size of `usize` is platform dependent. 

The issue seems to suggest that I should change the code so that the value is consistent on both platforms, but I'm hesitant to do so. At the very least it would require a new semver release as the value for 32-bit hosts would change.

For now, I've suggested that the ICU folks wrap the hasher in one that converts all `usize` to `u64`, which I think would address any immediate issues they have. Hopefully that means there's no urgent fire to put out.

This question is tangentially related to Rust's development as twox-hash is a dependency of the compiler through a few paths, but really I'm asking here to get a broader sense of how people would *expect* such a hasher crate to behave.
